lesson.title: Sorting Into Groups: Categorical Variables
lesson.summary: This section defines categorical variables as those that assign individuals to named groups rather than numeric values, and works through a worked example computing a proportion from the classroom dataset.
lesson.body:
Not every variable produces a number that makes sense to add up. A categorical variable, sometimes called a qualitative variable, is one that sorts each individual into one of a fixed set of named groups or categories, rather than assigning a numeric measurement. Eye color is categorical: a student's eyes might be brown, blue, or green, but there is no meaningful arithmetic you can do with those labels. You cannot average "brown" and "blue" the way you can average two quiz scores. Favorite subject, blood type, and yes or no survey answers are all categorical variables for the same reason: their possible values are names of groups, not quantities.

It is worth noting that categorical variables can sometimes be recorded using numbers, and this is a common source of confusion. A survey might code "yes" as 1 and "no" as 2, or a school might assign each department a numeric code. Those numbers are just labels standing in for categories, not real quantities. Averaging the department codes 1 and 2 to get 1.5 would produce a meaningless number, because there is no real department "1.5" and no real sense in which department 2 is twice as much department as department 1. The test for whether a variable is truly categorical is not whether its values happen to be written as digits, but whether those values name a group rather than measure an amount.

Add a categorical variable to the classroom dataset introduced earlier: gender, recorded for each of the 8 students as either female or male. Suppose the recorded values, one per student in order, are female, male, female, female, male, female, male, female. Counting them up, 5 of the 8 students are recorded as female and 3 of the 8 are recorded as male. Because this variable is categorical, the natural summary is not an average but a count or a proportion within each category. The proportion of students who are female is calculated by dividing the count by the total: 5 divided by 8 equals 0.625, or 62.5 percent. That proportion is a perfectly valid statistic, computed correctly, but notice that it required counting group membership, not adding up numeric measurements the way quiz score or height would be summarized.

Categorical variables are typically summarized with frequency tables, which list each category alongside its count or percentage, and displayed visually with bar charts or pie charts, where each category gets its own bar or slice. This is different from the tools used for quantitative variables, which is exactly why identifying a variable as categorical, right at the start of an analysis, matters so much. Choosing the right summary and the right graph both depend on getting this classification correct first. The next section turns to the other major type of variable, the quantitative variable, where genuine arithmetic like averaging finally becomes appropriate.
